<div id="bx-article">

<div class="bx-pills">
  <span class="bx-pill">Development</span>
  <span class="bx-pill">PHP</span>
  <span class="bx-pill">SEO</span>
</div>

<p>Hey! If your site has grown past one tidy sitemap.xml file, or you're already running separate sitemaps for posts, pages, and images, this one's for you.</p>

<p class="bx-lede">A PHP sitemap index generator sounds like a small addition once you already have real sitemap files, right up until Google quietly stops trusting the dates inside them. Built correctly it points search engines to every sitemap you actually have. Built carelessly, the one signal meant to tell Google what changed recently gets ignored completely, with nothing in Search Console ever telling you that happened.</p>

<div class="bx-section-head">
  <span class="bx-num">01</span>
  <h2 class="bx-h2" id="what-is-a-php-sitemap-index-generator">What Is a PHP Sitemap Index Generator?</h2>
  <div class="bx-rule"></div>
</div>

<p>A single sitemap file has a real ceiling: per the sitemap protocol that Google, Bing, and every other search engine follow, one sitemap can list at most 50,000 URLs and must stay under 50 KB per URL, adding up to a real 50 MB uncompressed size limit. <a href="https://library.linkbot.com/what-are-the-url-and-file-size-limits-for-sitemaps-and-how-can-large-sites-adapt/">The sitemap protocol's own documented limits</a> apply whether you hit the ceiling from URL count or from unusually long URLs and rich attributes.</p>

<p>A sitemap index file is the fix: instead of one file, you generate several smaller ones and list them inside a single index file using the real <code>sitemapindex</code> root tag. Per <a href="https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/sitemaps/large-sitemaps">Google's own documentation</a>, a sitemap index can reference up to 50,000 individual sitemaps, and every sitemap it lists has to live in the same directory as the index file or somewhere lower in the site hierarchy, never a different path entirely.</p>

<p><a href="https://searchengineland.com/guide/sitemap">Search Engine Land's own sitemap guide</a> makes the practical case well: as a site grows, maintaining one enormous file becomes fragile, one bad URL or a single slow database query can break the whole thing, while several smaller files behind one index isolate that risk to a single file instead of the entire site's crawl signals. That's the real operational reason a growing site reaches for this pattern long before it technically hits the URL ceiling.</p>

<div class="bx-tip">
  <p class="bx-tip-label">Tip</p>
  <p>Need the actual sitemap files this index will point to first? Our <a href="/build-xml-sitemap-generator-php/">XML sitemap generator in PHP guide</a> covers building those individual files.</p>
</div>

<div class="bx-section-head">
  <span class="bx-num">02</span>
  <h2 class="bx-h2" id="building-an-index-from-multiple-sitemap-types">Building an Index From Multiple Sitemap Types</h2>
  <div class="bx-rule"></div>
</div>

<p>The genuinely useful case for a PHP sitemap index generator isn't just splitting one huge sitemap by URL count, it's organizing several genuinely different sitemap files, posts, pages, and images being a common real split, under one index a search engine only has to fetch once. <a href="https://yoast.com/help/how-to-customize-the-sitemap-index/">Yoast SEO's own documentation confirms</a> this is exactly how a major, widely used real WordPress plugin structures its own sitemap index, referencing separate sitemaps for posts, pages, authors, categories, and tags rather than one combined file.</p>

<p>Here's a real function generating that structure from an array of sitemap entries, run straight from the PHP command line:</p>

<div class="bx-code-wrap">
  <div class="bx-code-title">SitemapIndexBuilder.php</div>
  <pre><code>buildSitemapIndex([
  ['loc' => 'https://brandella.in/sitemaps/posts.xml', 'lastmod' => '2026-09-01T10:15:00+00:00'],
  ['loc' => 'https://brandella.in/sitemaps/pages.xml', 'lastmod' => '2026-08-30T09:00:00+00:00'],
  ['loc' => 'https://brandella.in/sitemaps/images.xml', 'lastmod' => '2026-08-28T14:22:00+00:00'],
])
// -> a real &lt;sitemapindex&gt; XML document with 3 &lt;sitemap&gt; entries, one per file</code></pre>
</div>

<p>That output is a genuinely valid, minimal sitemap index, nothing more than three files listed with a location and a modification date each, which is all the format actually requires.</p>

<p>A real production PHP sitemap index generator usually pulls that array from somewhere other than a hard coded list, a database table tracking each generated sitemap file, or a directory scan filtered to real <code>.xml</code> and <code>.xml.gz</code> files. Either source works, as long as the same builder function validates every entry the same way regardless of where the array came from, so a bad row in a database can't produce broken output any more easily than a bad hand written array would.</p>

<div class="bx-section-head">
  <span class="bx-num">03</span>
  <h2 class="bx-h2" id="the-real-danger-of-a-fake-or-stale-lastmod">The Real Danger of a Fake or Stale Lastmod</h2>
  <div class="bx-rule"></div>
</div>

<p>This is the gotcha most PHP sitemap index generator tutorials skip entirely: the <code>lastmod</code> date is optional in the specification, but the moment you include it, Google holds it to a real standard. Per Google's own documentation, lastmod is only used "if it's consistently and verifiably accurate," checked against the page's actual modification date.</p>

<div class="bx-fact">
  <span class="bx-fact-label">Did You Know</span>
  <p>In July 2026, Google's own Gary Illyes was asked on Bluesky whether a site with unreliable modification dates should just drop the lastmod tag entirely. <a href="https://www.digitalapplied.com/blog/xml-sitemap-lastmod-hygiene-illyes-directive-seo-2026">His real answer</a>: "probably better off without the lastmods. at least you save a few bytes." Per the same source, Google's trust in lastmod is binary across an entire sitemap, not per URL, so a handful of fake dates can quietly get the whole file's dates ignored with no warning anywhere in Search Console.</p>
</div>

<p>That "binary trust" detail matters more than it sounds. It isn't a minor styling nitpick, since lastmod is one of the few real signals a site can use to hint which pages changed recently and deserve a fresh crawl sooner. Losing that signal across an entire sitemap because a handful of entries were stale or hand typed means every genuinely fresh page in that file loses its chance at faster recrawling too, not just the pages with bad dates.</p>

<p>The fix a PHP sitemap index generator can enforce directly: never type a lastmod value by hand. Read it straight off the actual file on disk instead.</p>

<div class="bx-code-wrap">
  <div class="bx-code-title">SitemapIndexBuilder.php</div>
  <pre><code>function realLastmodFromFile(string $path): string
{
    if (!file_exists($path)) {
        throw new InvalidArgumentException("Cannot read a real lastmod, file does not exist: $path");
    }
    return date(DATE_W3C, filemtime($path));
}</code></pre>
</div>

<p>A second, real check catches the other common mistake: a malformed date that isn't even valid in the first place.</p>

<div class="bx-code-wrap">
  <div class="bx-code-title">terminal</div>
  <pre><code>buildSitemapIndex([['loc' => '...', 'lastmod' => '07/16/2026']])
// -> InvalidArgumentException: Invalid lastmod value, not real W3C datetime format</code></pre>
</div>

  <script>(adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({});</script>
</div>

<div class="bx-section-head">
  <span class="bx-num">04</span>
  <h2 class="bx-h2" id="enforcing-the-real-sitemap-count-limit">Enforcing the Real Sitemap Count Limit</h2>
  <div class="bx-rule"></div>
</div>

<p>Per Google's own documentation, a sitemap index cannot list more than 50,000 individual sitemaps, the same style of hard ceiling as the 50,000 URL limit on each individual sitemap. A PHP sitemap index generator that reads its file list from a database or a directory scan should check this limit explicitly rather than assuming it will never be reached:</p>

<div class="bx-code-wrap">
  <div class="bx-code-title">SitemapIndexBuilder.php</div>
  <pre><code>if (count($sitemaps) > MAX_SITEMAPS_PER_INDEX) {
    throw new InvalidArgumentException(
        'A sitemap index cannot list more than ' . MAX_SITEMAPS_PER_INDEX . ' sitemaps, got ' . count($sitemaps)
    );
}</code></pre>
</div>

<p>Five real test cases against this exact builder function, run through the PHP command line rather than assumed to work: a standard three file index, a genuine rejection at 50,001 sitemaps, a genuine rejection of a malformed lastmod string, a real lastmod value pulled straight off an actual file's own modification time, and a real gzip round trip that decodes back to the exact original XML. All five pass against the real function, not a simulation of one.</p>

<p>Testing the limit at exactly 50,001 rather than some smaller stand in number matters here too. A test written against an arbitrary smaller threshold, say 10 or 100, would pass cleanly while quietly proving nothing about the actual real ceiling the specification defines, so this test suite generates the genuine boundary condition every time it runs.</p>

<div class="bx-section-head">
  <span class="bx-num">05</span>
  <h2 class="bx-h2" id="serving-it-with-real-gzip-compression">Serving It With Real Gzip Compression</h2>
  <div class="bx-rule"></div>
</div>

<p>Per <a href="https://www.php.net/manual/en/function.gzencode.php">PHP's own manual for the gzencode function</a>, a single real function call compresses a sitemap index into the gzip format search engines already know how to decompress, and per <a href="https://blogs.bing.com/webmaster/november-2016/increasing-the-size-limit-of-sitemaps-file-to-addr">Bing's own webmaster documentation</a>, a compressed sitemap still has to stay under the real 50 MB limit once decompressed, gzip only reduces what travels over the network.</p>

<div class="bx-code-wrap">
  <div class="bx-code-title">robots.php</div>
  <pre><code>header('Content-Encoding: gzip');
echo gzencode($xml, 9);</code></pre>
</div>

<p>Per <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Content-Encoding">MDN's own reference for the Content-Encoding header</a>, that header is what tells a client the body was compressed and how, so a real client decompresses it automatically rather than receiving raw compressed bytes it doesn't know what to do with. Leaving that header off while still sending compressed bytes is a real, easy mistake that breaks the response for anything that doesn't guess the encoding on its own.</p>

<p>Here's that exact real endpoint proven against a real running PHP server, first serving the plain XML with real lastmod values read off three actual files, then the gzip compressed version:</p>

<img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Terminal output showing a real curl request to a running PHP server returning a genuine HTTP 200 response with real lastmod values read directly from each sitemap file's own modification time">
</div>
<p class="bx-shot-caption">The real lastmod values come straight off each file's own modification time, not a hand typed guess.</p>

<div class="bx-shot">
<img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Terminal output showing a real curl request to the gzip compressed version of the endpoint, proving the decompressed content matches the plain XML exactly">
</div>
<p class="bx-shot-caption">The gzip compressed response decodes back to the identical original XML content.</p>

<div class="bx-section-head">
  <span class="bx-num">06</span>
  <h2 class="bx-h2" id="where-the-index-fits-with-your-other-sitemaps">Where the Index Fits With Your Other Sitemaps</h2>
  <div class="bx-rule"></div>
</div>

<p>If you're splitting one already large sitemap purely because it crossed the URL count ceiling, our <a href="/large-scale-xml-sitemaps-php-index-files/">guide to large scale XML sitemaps and index files in PHP</a> covers that specific chunking problem in depth. This article's focus is different on purpose: organizing genuinely separate sitemap types under one index, with lastmod values a PHP sitemap index generator can actually prove are accurate, rather than splitting a single content type by count alone.</p>

<p>Once the index file exists, two real places need to know about it. Your <a href="/dynamic-robots-txt-php/">dynamic robots.txt PHP script</a> should list it on its own <code>Sitemap:</code> line, and Search Console's own Sitemaps report needs only the index URL submitted, never every individual sitemap file one at a time.</p>

<div class="bx-tip">
  <p class="bx-tip-label">Tip</p>
  <p>Submitting just the index URL in Search Console is enough. Google follows every <code>loc</code> entry inside it automatically, so resubmitting each individual sitemap adds nothing.</p>
</div>

<p>Worth checking too: the same directory rule from section 01 applies just as strictly to a real deployment as it does on paper. A sitemap index served from the site root that lists a sitemap living on a completely different subdomain will genuinely be rejected, even though the file itself is perfectly valid XML. Keeping every generated file, index included, under one predictable real path avoids that entirely.</p>

<div class="bx-section-head">
  <span class="bx-num">07</span>
  <h2 class="bx-h2" id="common-pitfalls-with-a-php-sitemap-index-generator">Common Pitfalls With a PHP Sitemap Index Generator</h2>
  <div class="bx-rule"></div>
</div>

<p>Every real mistake covered so far comes back to the same handful of habits a working PHP sitemap index generator needs to get right, so here they are together as one checklist worth running through before this ever reaches production.</p>

<div class="bx-checklist">
  <li><b>Typing lastmod dates by hand.</b> Read the value from the actual file's own modification time instead, every single time.</li>
  <li><b>Assuming Google ignores individual bad dates.</b> Per Google's own team, the trust decision applies to the whole sitemap, not one bad entry.</li>
  <li><b>Never checking the 50,000 sitemap limit.</b> A directory scan or database query can grow past it silently without an explicit check.</li>
  <li><b>Skipping gzip on a genuinely large index.</b> It costs one function call and meaningfully reduces what search engines have to download.</li>
  <li><b>Submitting every individual sitemap to Search Console.</b> Submit the index URL alone; it already covers everything listed inside it.</li>
</div>

<p>For the surrounding pieces this pairs naturally with, <a href="/build-xml-sitemap-generator-php/">building an XML sitemap generator in PHP</a> and <a href="/indexnow-api-in-php/">the IndexNow API in PHP</a> are worth reading alongside this one, and <a href="/dynamic-robots-txt-php/">creating a dynamic robots.txt in PHP</a> covers exactly where this index file gets referenced for crawlers that check there first.</p>

<div class="bx-faq">
  <div class="bx-faq-item open">
    <button class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">1</span>What is a PHP sitemap index generator, and when do I need one?</button>
    <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>A script that generates a single file listing several individual sitemaps. You need one once a site has more than 50,000 URLs, or once you're maintaining separate sitemaps for different content types like posts, pages, and images.</p></div>
  </div>
  <div class="bx-faq-item open">
    <button class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">2</span>Why would Google ignore my lastmod dates?</button>
    <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Per Google's own team, lastmod is only trusted when it's consistently accurate against a page's real modification date. Fake or stale dates anywhere in a sitemap can get the whole file's dates ignored, with no warning shown anywhere in Search Console.</p></div>
  </div>
  <div class="bx-faq-item open">
    <button class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">3</span>How many sitemaps can one index file reference?</button>
    <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Up to 50,000, per Google's own documentation, the same real ceiling that applies to URLs inside each individual sitemap.</p></div>
  </div>
  <div class="bx-faq-item open">
    <button class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">4</span>Should I gzip my sitemap index and sitemap files?</button>
    <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Yes, it's explicitly supported and reduces what search engines download. Just remember the 50 MB size limit still applies to the uncompressed content, not the compressed file.</p></div>
  </div>
  <div class="bx-faq-item open">
    <button class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">5</span>Do I need to submit every individual sitemap to Search Console?</button>
    <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>No. Submit only the index file's own URL; Google follows every entry listed inside it automatically.</p></div>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="bx-learn">
  <h2 id="learn-today">Learn Today</h2>
  <div class="bx-learn-grid">
    <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">1</span><div><h4>Sitemap Index</h4><p>A single file listing several individual sitemaps under one sitemapindex root tag.</p></div></div>
    <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">2</span><div><h4>50,000 Sitemap Cap</h4><p>The real hard ceiling on how many sitemaps one index file can list.</p></div></div>
    <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">3</span><div><h4>Verifiable Lastmod</h4><p>Google only trusts a lastmod date it can confirm against the real page.</p></div></div>
    <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">4</span><div><h4>Gzip Round Trip</h4><p>A compressed sitemap should decode back to the exact original content.</p></div></div>
    <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">5</span><div><h4>Same Directory Rule</h4><p>A listed sitemap must live at or below the index file's own directory.</p></div></div>
    <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">6</span><div><h4>Multiple Sitemap Types</h4><p>Organizing posts, pages, and images as separate files under one index.</p></div></div>
  </div>
</div>

<script>
document.querySelectorAll('.bx-faq-item').forEach(function(item){
  var q = item.querySelector('.bx-faq-q');
  var a = item.querySelector('.bx-faq-a');
  a.style.maxHeight = a.scrollHeight + 'px';
  q.addEventListener('click', function(){
    var isOpen = item.classList.contains('open');
    if (isOpen) {
      item.classList.remove('open');
      a.style.maxHeight = '0px';
    } else {
      item.classList.add('open');
      a.style.maxHeight = a.scrollHeight + 'px';
    }
  });
});
</script>
